summary.text: 妈 means “mother” or “mama.” It combines 女, which contributes a female-related meaning, with 马, the simplified form of 馬, analyzed as a sound component.

formation.text: 妈 is a phonosemantic compound: 女 contributes a female-related meaning, while 馬 supplies a plausible sound cue. In the Zhengzhang Shangfang Old Chinese reconstruction, 媽 *maːʔ and 馬 *mraːʔ share an initial and broadly similar rhyme, although their vowels differ. 妈 is the standardized simplified form of 媽.

components.text: 女 contributes a female-related meaning in this character. No distinct earlier form for this component is established.
马 is the simplified form of 馬 within 妈. The historical sound comparison shows a similar initial and broad rhyme despite the vowel difference; modern Mandarin readings also resemble one another.

sound.text: In Zhengzhang Shangfang Old Chinese, 媽 *maːʔ and 馬 *mraːʔ share an initial and broadly similar rhyme, though their vowels differ; this supports a plausible phonetic relationship.
In modern Standard Mandarin, 马 mǎ and 妈 mā share an initial but differ in tone; this present-day resemblance alone does not establish their historical relationship.

history.text: The visible construction of 媽 is 女 plus 馬. It is not recorded in Shuowen, and no earlier paleographic form is established here.
In 妈, 馬 is written 马 as part of the standardized simplified form of 媽.

uncertainties.text: The early dictionary gloss for 媽 is “mother,” but its cited primary page image was not inspected, so the date of that attestation is not independently verified.

The phonetic analysis has a reported Zhengzhang Old Chinese comparison, but no matched comparison from another reconstruction system is available; modern Mandarin readings alone cannot establish the historical sound relationship.

senses.text: An early dictionary gloss cited for 媽 means “mother”; its date is not independently verified from the primary page.

senses.gloss: form of address for female elders, older women, and servants in northern usage
senses.text: Dictionary records include these address uses but do not date them or establish that they developed from the mother sense.
An excerpt lists an obsolete, single-attestation sense “mare,” without a dated citation establishing its relation to the mother sense.

limitations.text: The available senses do not establish a dated path among “mother,” the female-address uses, and “mare,” so no development is inferred.
A secondary account relates 媽 to 母 and proposes an older-language source, but the spoken-word history and any semantic path are not established here.
